land.text: Han took over the Old Chosŏn lands and established the Four Commanderies of Han in the western part of former Old Chosŏn

successors.note: Lelang, Lintun and Zhenfan in 108 BCE and Xuantu in 107 BCE (Four Commanderies of Han page). The commanderies are Han administrative units; Cliopatria draws no separate row for them, so the Han Dynasty (ea-02) and the additions batch (jk-02-x) carry the land from 108 BCE.

capitals.name: Wanggeom-seong (Pyongyang)
capitals.note: Wiman Joseon page: in 194 BCE Wi Man 'decided to locate his capital in Wanggeom-seong'; the Gojoseon page: 'the capital of Old Chosŏn was Wanggeom-seong (now Pyongyang) from at least the 2nd century BCE'. The seat before 194 BCE (King Jun's) is not on the pages; the dot is held at Wanggeom for 197-194 for want of a better place.

keyframe_review.note: -197..-127, 81,225 km2 (Pyongan and Hwanghae, about 123.8-128.1E, 37.6-41.3N). Neither page gives an area or a boundary: the Gojoseon page says only that the extent is debated ('since the 1980s and 1990s, South Korean scholarship has shifted the scope of Old Chosŏn to include territories in Manchuria') and that it lost '2000 li (800 kilometers) of territory' to Yan around 300 BCE. The shape stands as a core around Wanggeom (Pyongyang); the infobox area comparison is not possible. Unverified: page budget.

-126..-111, 81,296 km2, the same shape within 71 km2. The Wiman Joseon page puts the Han Canghai Commandery 'around 128-126 BCE' over 'the northern Korean Peninsula and southern Manchuria'; the page does not say it took land from Wiman Joseon proper and the commandery was abolished within two years, so the Cliopatria shape is not changed.

correction.text: the same shape, for -110..-108 only: 'Wanggeom fell in 108 BCE' and the land passed to the Han commanderies; Cliopatria's row runs to -92

keyframe_review.note: -110..-92 in Cliopatria (81,320 km2). The state ends in 108 BCE ('In 108 BCE, the Han dynasty, under Emperor Wu of Han, invaded and conquered Wiman Joseon'); the years -107..-92 belong to the Han commanderies (Lelang, Lintun, Zhenfan, Xuantu), whose shape is the same land. Years change, not the outline.

region.text: Old Chosŏn around Wanggeom-seong (Pyongyang), the realm Cliopatria draws from 197 BCE

ledger.note: 197 BCE: Gojoseon enters the map under King Jun. The Gojoseon page gives no founding year beyond the legend ('established in 2333 BCE by Tan'gun') and its first dated event is the war with Yan 'around 300 BCE'; -197 is Cliopatria's first shape and the pages are silent on the realm's extent that year.

194 BCE: Wi Man overthrows King Jun and founds Wiman Joseon. 'In 194 BCE, the ruling dynasty of Old Chosŏn was overthrown by Wi Man' (the same page elsewhere says he was posted to the frontier 'In 195 BCE'); King Jun 'fled to Jin in the south of the Korean Peninsula'. The state, its land and its colour continue.
194 BCE: Wi Man makes Wanggeom-seong (Pyongyang) his capital. 'In 194 BC, he established Wiman Chosŏn and decided to locate his capital in Wanggeom-seong.'

region.text: Wiman Joseon's realm around Wanggeom, invaded from the west

ledger.note: 109 BCE: Emperor Wu of Han invades Wiman Joseon. 'in 109 BC, Emperor Wu of Han invaded Wiman Chosŏn near the Luan River' (the Gojoseon page says 'near the Liao River'); 'After a year of battle, Wanggeom-seong was captured'. The page does not say which ground the Han took in 109, so the whole realm is the zone.
108 BCE: Wanggeom falls and the fighting ends. 'Wanggeom fell in 108 BCE.'

region.text: the Old Chosŏn lands, where Han set up the commanderies

ledger.note: 108 BCE: Han takes Old Chosŏn and sets up Lelang, Lintun and Zhenfan. 'When Old Chosŏn was defeated in 108 BCE, three commanderies were established in its place: Lelang, Lintun, and Zhenfan'; Xuantu followed in 107 BCE. The Gojoseon page puts them 'in the western part of former Old Chosŏn' and Wiman Joseon places them in 'the Liaodong Peninsula and the northwestern Korean Peninsula'.

108 BCE: Wiman Joseon falls and Gojoseon ends. 'In 108 BCE, the Han dynasty, under Emperor Wu of Han, invaded and conquered Wiman Joseon'; the Wiman Joseon page dates the dynasty '194-108 BC'. Its land becomes the Han commanderies; the south (Jin) and the peoples beyond stay outside Han rule.

wars.name: Han invasion of Wiman Joseon

zones.text: the realm of Wiman Joseon, from the river frontier to Wanggeom

wars.outcome: Han victory: Wanggeom fell in 108 BCE, Wiman Joseon ended and Han set up the commanderies of Lelang, Lintun and Zhenfan (108) and Xuantu (107).
wars.note: 'in 109 BC, Emperor Wu of Han invaded Wiman Chosŏn near the Luan River'; 'After a year of battle, Wanggeom-seong was captured and Wiman Chosŏn was destroyed.' The Gojoseon page suggests scholars think Han feared Old Chosŏn 'would ally with the Xiongnu against the Han' (the Xiongnu are a Cliopatria neighbour to -111). The two pages disagree on the river (Liao or Luan).

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line on either page; the extent of Old Chosŏn is itself debated (the Gojoseon page notes the Manchurian scope favoured since the 1980s). The Cliopatria shape is a core around Pyongyang.

sources.title: Gojoseon
sources.note: Identity, capital, 194 and 108 BCE, the Yan war c. 300 BCE, the Xiongnu worry; no area.

sources.title: Wiman Joseon
sources.note: 194-108 BCE, Wanggeom-seong, the 109-108 war, Canghai Commandery c. 128-126 BCE.

sources.title: Four Commanderies of Han
sources.note: The commanderies set up in 108/107 BCE and their later history; also used for Dongye.

notes: Cliopatria's Gojoseon (Wikidata Q28405) shares its Wikidata id with the Joseon dynasty row (joseon, 1395-1897); they are different states (Old Joseon, legendary 2333 BCE to 108 BCE on its page, against the Joseon row of 1395-1897), so no merge; the shared id looks like a Wikidata mix-up and the joseon row is another batch's dossier. Cliopatria's three shapes are the same outline (81.2-81.3 thousand km2) to -92, but the state ends in 108 BCE: the keyframe verdict -110 shortens the years; -107..-92 is Han commanderies land (Lelang, Lintun, Zhenfan, Xuantu), for which Cliopatria has no row (counterparts_needing_dossiers: lelang-commandery, the Han commanderies in Korea, for jk-02-x). The state is older than the map shows: the pages give a legendary 2333 BCE foundation, a Gija Joseon of 1122 BCE that 'many modern experts deny', and a war with Yan around 300 BCE, but no territory, so the dossier starts at Cliopatria's first year (-197) with a confidence-1 found event. The 194 BCE change of dynasty (Gija/King Jun to Wi Man) is a rename, not a new state. King Jun's flight south to Jin (Gojoseon page; Samhan page 'around 194-180 BCE') is recorded in the Korean Jin and Mahan notes, not as a territorial event. Neighbour korean-jin is the state to the south; the Wiman Joseon page says King Ugeo 'prevented the Jin state from communicating with the Han dynasty'. The area could not be compared with an infobox: neither page gives one. Pages disagree on where the Han army crossed in 109 BCE (Liao River on the Gojoseon page, Luan River on Wiman Joseon). Page budget: 3 pages (two of the state's own plus the Four Commanderies page opened for Dongye). The war with Yan around 300 BCE ('Around 300 BCE, Old Chosŏn lost significant western territory after a war with the Yan state'; 'the loss of 2000 li (800 kilometers) of territory', Gojoseon page) falls before the dossier's start and the page does not place the land, so it is not a war entry (moved from wars to these notes by the jk-02-a reviewer).
